title: GitHub API Rate Limit Exceeded? Fix 403 and 429 Errors
summary: GitHub API rate limits cap your request quota. Understand why exhausting them breaks nightly syncs and how the limits work.
body_markdown:
## Run the Same GitHub Calls with Activepieces


### Setting up the connection


Activepieces lets you run the nightly sync's GitHub calls as a visual flow instead of a script you host. It changes none of GitHub's limits, so the rules from the runbook still apply to every step you build.


Setup's where it earns its place.


Activepieces ships a GitHub integration (its name for a connector) with triggers and actions, one of the 750 integrations counted in its open source monorepo, whose core is under the MIT licence, so the GitHub triggers and actions are source you can read, not a vendor's description.


If no template covers your case, you can describe it in plain language to the built-in AI chat, and it builds and publishes a runnable flow instead of returning a template search result: ask it for a flow that opens a ticket and pings a channel when a sync step hits a 403 or 429, and the flow comes back published, not as a search hit.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production, and every plan, the free one included, allows unlimited flows.


Once you add a connection in Activepieces and authenticate it with GitHub, every step in the flow reuses that credential.


That means no token handling in your own code and no rotation script to maintain, and when a token is revoked you fix one connection instead of hunting through cron jobs.


### What a workflow looks like in the builder


The screenshot below shows the shape of a flow in the builder canvas. A trigger sits at the top, two OpenAI steps feed a WordPress step at the bottom, and that last step's selected, which means WordPress will receive processed data from two AI sources.


Its panel shows an action and a connection, with fields filled by references to earlier steps.


Your GitHub flow looks the same: a connection picked from a dropdown, and inputs wired to the output of the step before. The takeaway's that each step's one call, so you can count the calls a run makes by counting the steps.


### Limits and retries still apply


That counting matters because the failure mode's unchanged. A flow that loops over every repository and calls GitHub for each one spends your quota exactly as a script would, and a 403 or 429 from GitHub surfaces as a failed step.


Activepieces can retry a failed step, but a retry's another request against the same limit. Retrying immediately into an exhausted quota makes the outage longer.


Check the response headers GitHub documents for when the limit resets, and build the wait into the flow rather than relying on blind retries.


### When to keep the work in code


Know where this approach stops. For large bulk reads, such as walking every issue across a big organization, raw API code's the better tool. You control pagination and how fast you consume the budget, and a visual loop gives you less of that control.


Use Activepieces for event-driven triggers and modest per-run actions, and keep the heavy reads in code.
